plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the true Tunguska event of 30 June 1908: Semyon Semenov is thrown from his porch 65 km away, herders lose their herds, nights glow over Europe, and in 1927 Leonid Kulik finds 80 million flattened trees but no crater; the twist is that the trees at the centre still stand because the space rock exploded in the air and never landed.

beats.say: 1908, Siberia. A man on his porch was thrown off by the sky.
Thrown by the sky? Mothwick, skies don't push people.
His name was Semyon Semenov, at the Vanavara trading post.
This is true, Odo. He told scientists every word later.
June thirtieth, just after seven in the morning. A clear summer day.
The sky split in two. Fire filled the whole north.
It was so hot my shirt felt like it was burning.
Then came a bang, and a wind that knocked him down.
How far away was the fire? Right next to him?
About sixty-five kilometres away. Remember that number.
Sixty-five kilometres, and it still burned his shirt.
Reindeer herders said whole herds and tents were gone.
The trees fell like grass. The forest was lying down.
In London, nights were so bright people read papers at midnight.
London? That's on the other side of the world!
But Siberia was far, and Russia was at war soon after.
For nineteen years, no scientist went to look.
Nineteen years? The trees just lay there all that time?
Lying there, Odo. Waiting for someone to ask the right question.
Subscribe for a new true story every day. Now the strangest part.
In 1927, Leonid Kulik finally walked into the forest.
We are looking for a crater. A huge stone from space.
He found millions of trees flat on the ground, all pointing outward.
About eighty million trees. Over two thousand square kilometres.
So he followed them to the middle. To the crater.
At the centre, the trees were not lying down at all.
They stood upright, burned and stripped bare, like telegraph poles.
There is no crater. There is no stone. Nothing.
No hole? Then what flattened eighty million trees?
Kulik searched the swamps for ten more years. He found no stone.
Every expert said a crater must be here. I dug and dug.
Think, Odo. Why would the middle trees still stand?
Because the blow came from straight above them?
Exactly. Scientists now think a space rock exploded in the air.
Five to ten kilometres up. It never touched the ground.
So there was nothing left to find. It became heat and wind.
Under the blast, trees were hit from above and kept standing.
Further out, the wind pushed every tree flat and outward.
And sixty-five kilometres away, it burned a man's shirt.
It is the biggest impact event in recorded history.
And almost nobody lived there. That is why so few died.
Over a city, Odo, there would have been no city left.
Today June thirtieth is Asteroid Day, because of Tunguska.
Telescopes now watch the sky for rocks like the one at Tunguska.
I'll still sit on porches. Just not facing north.
If this one got you, the Christmas ghost army of Edgehill is next.
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

long.title: Siberia 1908: 80 Million Trees Fell, No Crater | True Story
long.description:
Previous true story: https://youtu.be/1ntmNRGVkKg
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

"Sixty-five kilometres away, the sky burned his shirt." — Odo

A true story from Siberia, 30 June 1908: a fireball over the Tunguska river flattened about 80 million trees over 2,000 km². Semyon Semenov at the Vanavara trading post felt the heat and was thrown from his porch. When Leonid Kulik finally reached the site in 1927, he found no crater, and at the centre the trees were still standing.
